h: פּוּרִים, מַאֲמָר ח׳ Purim — Maamar Ches

p: The entire episode of the miracle of the Megillah
for the beginning of the salvation,
כְּטוֹב לֵב הַמֶּלֶךְ בַּיָּיִן [אֶסְתֵּר א, י]
when the heart of the king was merry with wine" (Esther 1:10);
that wherever it says in the Megillah
it speaks also of the King of kings,
the Holy One, blessed is He,
for it serves as both sacred and mundane;
for the whole matter of the Megillah
of the sprouting of the salvation
toward the building of the Beis HaMikdash,
which is the place of the korbanos and the libations,
וְנֶאֱמַר [בַּמִּדְבָּר כח, ב] אֶת קָרְבָּנִי לַחְמִי לְאִשַּׁי
and it is said (Bamidbar 28:2): "My offering, My bread for My fires,"
while your Master's table is empty."
And the beginning of the sprouting of the salvation
was in the killing of Vashti,
to destroy the seed of Nevuchadnetzar,
the very opening of the Megillah
מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר [יְשַׁעְיָה יד, כב] וְקַמְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם וְגוֹ׳
is what is said (Yeshayahu 14:22), "I will rise up against them," etc.,
"and I will cut off from Bavel," etc.
Therefore it is written, "On the seventh day,
when the heart of the king was merry with wine" —
the Holy One, blessed is He
(and so it is written in Midrash Abba Gurion (parshah 1):
"When the heart of the king was merry with wine" —
כְּטוֹב לִבּוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּ׳)
as the heart of the Holy One, blessed is He, was good, etc.),
for there was awakened from Above
the merit of the korbanos and the libations,
as they said in the Gemara (Megillah 12b):
was said on account of the korbanos, etc.,
invoked the merit of the korbanos.
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הָיָה זְמַן הַפְּקִידָה אָז
For in truth it was then the time of remembrance,
now surely they will no longer be redeemed" —
he brought out the vessels of the Mikdash, etc.
the time of the End would have been reckoned so,
the four hundred years were reckoned
and He was "leaping over the mountains,"
It is written "in its time" and it is written "I will hasten it" —
if they merit, "I will hasten it."
וְרַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה קִטְרוּג שֶׁל הָמָן
And only because there was Haman's accusation
לָכֵן לֹא הָיָה בִּיכוֹלֶת לִהְיוֹת אָז
was it not possible that there then be
the building of the Beis HaMikdash in actual fact,
but not a thing that divides the kingdom,
and what is that? The building of the Beis HaMikdash.
עִם כָּל זֶה נִבְנָה אָז בְּהֶעְלֵם
Even so, there was built then, in concealment,
the preparation for building the Beis HaMikdash,
for she said, "And so I will go in to the king,
which is not according to the law" (Esther 4:16),
and from this was born Daryavesh son of Esther,
And all of Esther's pleas at the wine-feast —
"If I have found favor in your eyes, O King,
and if it please the King,
תִּנָּתֶן לִי נַפְשִׁי וְגוֹ׳ [שָׁם ז, ג]
let my life be given me," etc. (ibid. 7:3),
and likewise, "and the thing seem right
all of it was, in her inner intent,
prayer to the Holy One, blessed is He,
while on the surface her words appeared
as if she were speaking to Achashverosh;
just as the Rama MiPano explained
[עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת מַאֲמַר אֵם כָּל חַי ח״א סִימָן ז]
(Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Em Kol Chai, part 1, siman 7)
regarding Nechemiah, where it is written (Nechemiah 2:4):
"And I prayed to the God of Heaven,
and I said to the king," etc. —
that although we do not find
only the words he spoke to the king,
his intent in them was prayer to Hashem Yisbarach.
So too here, Esther's words were
words of prayer to Hashem Yisbarach,
yet they were heard in the ears of Achashverosh
as though she were asking of him;
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ [אֶסְתֵּר רַבָּה שָׁם] שֶׁמְּשַׁמֵּשׁ קֹדֶשׁ וָחוֹל:
and this is what they said (Esther Rabbah, ibid.), that it serves as both sacred and mundane.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Divrei Soferim 38 — “Corresponding to Achashverosh's first feast, the beginning of the cure through his drunkenness when Vashti was killed, and its completion at Esther's wine-feast … Haman drank the cup of poison.” Rav Tzadok there frames the same two feasts as the start and finish of one cure, and adds the contrast within the second feast: the same wine was Haman's downfall and Esther's joy.

paragraphs.text: Beitzah 20b — “Abba Shaul expressed it another way: If, where your hearth is closed, your Master's hearth is open, then where your hearth is open, is it not right that your Master's hearth should be open? It is indeed fitting that your table should not be full while your Master's table is empty.” The discussion concerns festival offerings: when the person may prepare festival food, offerings for the Divine altar should likewise be possible. Rav Tzadok uses the table image to relate the royal wine feasts to the remembered merit of the altar's offerings and libations.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 10b — “Rabbi Yonasan opened his exposition from: 'I shall rise against them ... and cut off from Bavel name, remnant, offspring, and descendant, says Hashem.' 'Name' is its script; 'remnant' is its language; 'offspring' is its kingship; and 'descendant' is Vashti.” The Gemara explicitly connects Vashti's removal with the ending of Bavel's dynasty. Rav Tzadok reads that beginning of Esther's story as the first concealed preparation for rebuilding the Temple that Bavel had destroyed.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 32 — “This feast is the feast of the King of the world … only in outward guise did they enjoy the wicked one's banquet; in truth they enjoyed the banquet of the King of the world.” Rav Tzadok there reads the whole seven-day feast through “the king” unqualified, adding that the seven days built a complete structure of the cure, finished on the seventh “when the king's heart was merry.”

paragraphs.text: Midrash Abba Guryon, chapter 1, on Esther 1:10 — “Rabbi Yudan and Rabbi Levi said in Rabbi Yochanan's name: Wherever the Megillah says 'King Ahasuerus,' the verse speaks of Ahasuerus. Wherever it says simply 'the king,' it speaks of the King of kings. 'When the king's heart was merry with wine'—when the Holy One's heart was merry with the wine of Torah.” The precise original passage, in Buber's Sifrei DeAggadeta edition, includes 'the wine of Torah.' Rav Tzadok develops the sacred wine image here through the merit of Temple offerings and libations; that development should be distinguished from the Midrash's own wording.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 12b — “The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, did they ever offer You year-old lambs as Israel offered You? Did they offer You two turtledoves? Did they build You an earthen altar? Did they serve before You in priestly garments containing 'beryl, onyx, and jasper'? Did they stir the blood before You, or mix meal-offerings before You? Did they prepare a table before You?” Rabbi Levi introduces this interpretation by saying that the entire verse naming the seven advisers is expounded through offerings. The angels' appeal to Israel's service is the explicit textual basis for the maamar's claim that sacrificial merit awakens the concealed rescue.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 11b — “After the reckoning of seventy years, he said: Now they will certainly no longer be redeemed. He brought out the Temple vessels and used them.” The discussion first identifies Belshazzar's mistaken reckoning and then Ahasuerus's different but likewise mistaken reckoning. At 11b:12 the latter similarly brings out the vessels; the Satan then dances among them, and Vashti is killed. Rav Tzadok's claim that Israel's merit could have made an earlier time effective is his interpretation of the potential hidden within that period.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 98a — “Rabbi Alexandri said: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi posed a contradiction: It is written, 'in its time,' and it is written, 'I shall hasten it.' If they merit, 'I shall hasten it'; if they do not merit, 'in its time.'” Both expressions are in Isaiah 60:22. The distinction permits Rav Tzadok's account of a possible earlier redemption while preserving an appointed ultimate time.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 15b — “'What is your request? Up to half the kingdom, and it shall be done'—half the kingdom, not the whole kingdom, and not something that creates a division in the kingdom. What was that? The rebuilding of the Temple.” The Gemara makes the Temple the excluded request. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes the concealed preparation achieved through Esther from an immediate, openly authorized rebuilding.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 15a — “'I shall come to the king, not according to the law'—Rabbi Abba said: It was not according to the established rule, for until now each day was under compulsion, but now it was voluntary. 'As I am lost, I am lost'—just as I was lost to my father's house, so I shall be lost to you.” The source distinguishes Esther's compelled position from the voluntary approach undertaken to rescue Israel. The maamar places that act within its account of hidden preparation for the Temple's future restoration.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 13:5; Ezra 6:14–15 — “Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon said: The last Darius was Esther's son, pure from his mother and impure from his father.” This is the Midrashic genealogy used by the maamar. Ezra 6:14–15 separately records the Temple's building under the Persian royal decrees and its completion on the third of Adar in Darius's sixth regnal year. Both originals were retrieved; the genealogy is presented as the Midrash's tradition.

paragraphs.text: Rema MiPano, Asarah Maamaros, Im Kol Chai I:7 — “When Artaxerxes said to Nechemyah, 'Why is your face sad?' it is written, 'I prayed to the God of heaven.' Is it possible that between the king's question and Nechemyah's answer there was time to pray, even a short prayer? What, then, was his prayer? The very words he was saying before the king, with his heart directed to Heaven. And so too with Esther. This plainly teaches the people of Yehudah to take counsel within ourselves so that Hashem is always before us, and our words flow before Him in appeasement, request, and all our needs.” The original expressly includes Esther as well as Nechemyah. Rav Tzadok is therefore applying the Rema MiPano's own stated example, interpreting the court's spoken requests as inward prayer at the same moment.
